<reflection>
- The second experiment (S=1.0 M, cat=0.05 M, P=0.0 M) provided additional kinetic data. By combining the negative log-likelihood (NLL) values from both runs (approximated by summation), the cumulative NLL indicates that most mechanisms (except M4 and M5) fit the data reasonably well, with M7 having the best cumulative fit (-71.43), followed closely by M6, M8, M13, and M2. M3 has a notably worse cumulative NLL (-66.57), suggesting it is less plausible but not entirely ruled out. M4 and M5 have large positive NLL values and are effectively excluded.
- The aim of the second turn was to discriminate among mechanisms by probing a regime with lower substrate and higher catalyst to enhance sensitivity to dimerization and deactivation pathways. This was partially successful, as the relative ordering of models shifted slightly, but significant ambiguity remains among many candidates.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To further discriminate among the remaining mechanisms, I propose an experiment that introduces product initially. This will test for reversible product formation and product inhibition, which are features present in many mechanisms (e.g., reversible steps in M1-M3, product inhibition in M12 and M17, and product-dependent deactivation in M12, M17). By adding product, we can break symmetries between mechanisms that differ in their response to product concentration. I choose moderate substrate (1.5 M) and moderate catalyst (0.02 M) to avoid extreme saturation or depletion, while the product concentration (0.2 M) is significant enough to perturb the kinetics. This condition explores a new dimension (non-zero product) and lies in an intermediate regime relative to previous experiments, ensuring that mechanistic differences remain observable without driving the system to limits where all models behave similarly.
</hypothesis>
